display.title: The Unimaginable Great Reward
display.summary_short: Why we cannot imagine the goodness of the days of Moshiach, and how the Rambam exposed jealous court doctors who claimed to cure a man blind from birth.
display.summary_long: The storyteller explains the Ani Maamin: the thirteen principles of faith come from the Rambam's introduction to Perek Chelek, and the Rambam teaches that it is not enough to believe Moshiach will come; we must eagerly look forward to it, like waiting for a special package, or like the Chofetz Chaim, who kept a special suit ready for Moshiach. But how can we wait for something we cannot picture? Chazal say one moment in the World to Come is greater than all the pleasures of this world, and the Rambam compares explaining it to teaching colors to someone born blind. That reminds him of a story: the Rambam was the sultan's favorite doctor, and jealous court doctors claimed they could cure a man blind from birth, something the Rambam said no medicine could do. Before the king and two sworn witnesses they treat the man, who then counts fingers correctly. The Rambam asks one more test: he holds up blue and red cloths, and the man names the colors at once. A man who had never seen could not know their names, so the plot is exposed and the Rambam stays the king's chief doctor.
display.lesson: The good of the days of Moshiach is beyond anything we can imagine, so we should look forward to it eagerly and bring it closer with Torah and mitzvos.

sources_cited.note: Belief in Moshiach includes awaiting his coming.
